passage: I'm Rashmi. In my family, tears were for private rooms; my father would say "Be strong" and that was that. When Yash's grandmother passed away, his whole family cried openly at the funeral, hugging and wailing, and I stood stiff at the edge, thinking I ought to be doing something. Yash noticed and whispered, "You don't have to cry, my family just does it that way." I felt hot with embarrassment. Later I said, "In my house we didn't show it. It doesn't mean I felt less." He said, "I thought maybe you didn't care." We both laughed sadly. I still don't cry easily, but I hold his hand now, and he doesn't take it as coldness.

qa.a: They told each other what showing or hiding tears meant in their own families, and asked instead of assuming.

passage:
Tuesday night
Tanvir cried at work today. After the client call where they cancelled his whole project, he went to the pantry, and when I walked in, his eyes were streaming. He turned away fast.
Then Rakesh walked in behind me, saw him, and said, "Arre, be a man, yaar," laughing. Tanvir went red and left.
I kept thinking about it all afternoon. In my family, the men cry at every wedding and funeral and nobody blinks. In Tanvir's, maybe not. Maybe he was ashamed. Maybe he was just furious. I didn't know, and neither did Rakesh.
So at five I messaged him: "Hey, that call sounded brutal. How are you feeling?" He wrote back: "Angry, mostly. Two years of work. The crying just happens when I'm angry, and I hate it." I said I get the same, and that it's nothing to be embarrassed about. He sent back a thumbs-up and "thanks, needed that".
Tomorrow I'm going to say something to Rakesh.
Sharmila

qa.a: 'Arre, be a man, yaar.'

qa.a: Tanvir felt mostly angry about losing two years of work, and embarrassed that anger makes him cry.

qa.a: Sharmila messaged privately to ask how he felt instead of assuming, and reassured him the tears were nothing to be embarrassed about.

qa.q: How did Rakesh's joke affect Tanvir?
qa.a: It embarrassed him, turning him red and making him leave, adding shame to his anger.

passage: At the wedding in a village near Gorakhpur, the moment came for the bride to leave. Sharmila's cousin Pinki clung to her mother and wept loudly, shoulders heaving, and her aunts wept with her. Joseph, Sharmila's colleague from Kochi, stood frozen by the jeep. At weddings in his family, everyone smiled for photos and saved tears for home. He leaned over to Sharmila and whispered, worried, "Is she being forced? She looks heartbroken." Sharmila understood why he'd think so. "In our family, the bride crying at bidaai is expected. Leaving home is a real grief, even when she's happy with the marriage. But you're right to ask; I'd never assume for her either." Later, at the new house, Sharmila found Pinki laughing with her husband's sisters, eyes still puffy. "Were you okay at bidaai?" Sharmila asked quietly. Pinki squeezed her hand. "Sad to leave Ma. Happy about everything else. Both." Sharmila went back and told Joseph, who looked relieved.

passage: At Yara's farewell lunch in a Toronto engineering firm, the team gathered round a lopsided cake. When Kaito stood to thank her for two years of mentoring, his face went bright red and his voice stayed flat. "Look at Kaito, furious we're losing her," someone joked. Yara, meanwhile, was crying openly, dabbing her eyes and laughing. In her family, tears at goodbyes were expected, a sign of respect. In Kaito's, his dad had always said a man keeps his face steady at work. A new intern whispered, "Guess she's the emotional one and he's the robot." Later, by the coat rack, Yara didn't guess. "Your face went red during the speech. Were you embarrassed, or upset about something?" Kaito shrugged, then smiled. "Mostly embarrassed. I hate speeches. And sad, honestly. I just don't show it the way you do." Yara hugged the cake box. "Both work," she said.
